title: It's Always Better to Know
author: David Didau
summary: David Didau recounts teaching a demonstration Year 10 poetry lesson using hinge-point questions, where a majority of students picked the wrong answer because they'd been distracted by surface wording, revealing they hadn't grasped the intended comparison between two poems. When the class teacher afterward called the lesson a 'failure' because students hadn't gotten the hinge question right, Didau pushed back: the point of teaching is to accurately know what students have and haven't learned, not to engineer a smooth-looking performance in the moment. He generalizes from this to argue that most teachers ask too few questions of too few students, mistaking a single confident volunteer's correct answer for evidence the whole class understands. His central claim is that many teachers are, consciously or not, reluctant to probe understanding too carefully because discovering that students don't understand feels like a personal failure -- when in fact the more accurate a teacher's read of student understanding, the better positioned they are to address misconceptions and consolidate learning.
points: Didau's reframe of a 'failed' hinge-point lesson: the lesson succeeded precisely because it revealed a real misconception (confusion caused by the word 'both'), which is the entire point of checking for understanding.

His critique of common classroom practice -- taking the first raised hand as evidence the whole class understands -- is backed by his own habit of quietly checking a neighboring student, who typically has no idea what was just said.

Didau's core psychological claim: teachers avoid rigorous checks for understanding not from laziness but from a self-protective instinct, since discovering a lesson didn't land can feel like a personal failure.

The piece closes on a reframed cost-benefit: probing understanding may feel exposing in the moment, but the alternative -- teaching on for false assurance -- guarantees the same misconception resurfaces later, undetected.
quotes: I tried to explain that the point of teaching is to know, the best of our ability, what students have and haven't learned. The point isn't that students can perform in the here and now, it's that their understanding should be secure elsewhere and later.
All too often, lessons end without teachers having done anything designed to give them a clear idea about what students think.

I've lost count of the times I've seen teachers ask a question, take the first answer given (often from a student with their hand up) as evidence that the class's understanding is secure, and move on.
I make a habit of asking the student next to me if they a) heard the answer their classmate gave and b) if they understood what had been said. Typically, they have little idea of what has happened.
I've come to the tentative conclusion that many teachers are nervous of carefully probing their class's understanding in case they find out students don't know or understand what has been taught.

The difference between my poetry lesson and many of the lessons I observe is that I knew students hadn't understood whereas often teacher either have no idea of their class's understanding or, worse, have convinced themselves through insufficient sampling that students know things they're actually still very confused about.

It may feel exposing to teach in a way that reveals students' understanding, it may feel like a risk to really probe how many students have actually grasped what you've tried to teach but, whether they do or they don't, it's always better to know.
